title: Cache Miss Classification — the 3 Cs
summary: Compulsory, capacity, and conflict misses — the framework that tells you which fix actually addresses a given miss.

slides.subTitle: Not all misses are alike
slides.markdown:
Every cache miss falls into one of three categories, each with a different root cause and a different fix: **compulsory** (first-touch, unavoidable), **capacity** (the working set doesn't fit), and **conflict** (placement collisions that a differently-shaped cache of the same size wouldn't have).

This matters because "the miss rate is too high" isn't actionable on its own — knowing *which* C dominates tells you whether to add associativity, grow the cache, prefetch earlier, or accept the miss as unavoidable.

slides.subTitle: The cold-start cost
slides.markdown:
A **compulsory** (or cold) miss happens on the very first access to a block — it was never in cache before, so no placement or capacity policy could have prevented it. Even an infinitely large, fully associative cache still takes this miss once per block.

The only real mitigation is **prefetching** — predicting an address will be needed and fetching it before the CPU asks, turning a would-be compulsory miss into a hit by arriving early instead of avoiding the fetch entirely.

slides.subTitle: The working set doesn't fit
slides.markdown:
A **capacity** miss happens when the cache simply isn't large enough to hold everything the program is actively reusing — even a fully associative cache of that size would evict the same block eventually, because there's nowhere else to put it.

The fix is a bigger cache (more capacity at that level) or restructuring the program to shrink its working set — for example, tiling a loop so it touches a smaller chunk of data at a time (cross-link: cache-conscious-programming).

slides.subTitle: Misses associativity would have avoided
slides.markdown:
A **conflict** miss happens when two blocks map to the same set and evict each other, even though the cache overall has spare capacity elsewhere. A fully associative cache of the *same size* would not have taken this miss — it's purely a side effect of limited placement freedom.

The fix is more associativity (more ways per set), since that's the exact knob that controls how many blocks can coexist in one set before one must be evicted.

slides.subTitle: Direct-mapped vs associative
slides.markdown:
Running the identical access trace through two cache shapes exposes the difference.

![The same access trace producing different miss types under direct-mapped vs associative caches](assets/miss-classification-trace.svg)

Both caches take the same compulsory misses on first touch. But the direct-mapped cache also takes conflict misses the associative cache entirely avoids — same trace, same total capacity, different placement freedom.

slides.subTitle: Coherence misses
slides.markdown:
Multiprocessor systems add a **4th C: coherence** misses — a line is invalidated not because *this* core evicted it, but because another core wrote to the same address, forcing this core's copy to be refetched to stay consistent.

This is a fundamentally different mechanism from the original 3 Cs: it's driven by cross-core sharing, not this core's own access pattern or cache shape. It's covered in full in cache-coherence-protocols, since it needs the MESI/coherence-protocol machinery to explain properly.

slides.subTitle: Matching the fix to the cause
slides.markdown:
| Dominant C | Signature | Matching fix |
|---|---|---|
| Compulsory | High on first pass over new data, independent of cache size | Prefetching |
| Capacity | Miss rate stays high even at high associativity | Bigger cache, or shrink the working set |
| Conflict | Miss rate drops sharply when associativity increases at the same total size | More ways per set |

**How to decide:** simulate (or reason about) the same access pattern at increasing associativity, holding total size fixed. If misses barely change, they're capacity misses your working set genuinely needs more room for. If misses drop sharply, they were conflict misses the original placement was too rigid to avoid.
